content.title: About
content.content: Cake and cupcakes are baked goods often flavored with spices such as cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, and clove. These spices give the desserts a distinctive aroma, enhance flavor complexity, and make the treat more satisfying.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cinnamon is one of the oldest spices and was used in ancient Egypt to flavor breads and cakes.
Nutmeg can be toxic in large amounts, so it is added to baked goods only in small doses.
Ginger was introduced to Europe from Asia in the Middle Ages and quickly became popular in holiday cupcakes.
Clove is a traditional ingredient in Christmas and New Year cakes in Northern Europe.
A blend of several spices in a single recipe is called "five-spice" and is typical for classic English cakes.

items.title: Antioxidant effect
items.content: Cinnamon, ginger, and clove are rich in polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Ginger and nutmeg stimulate gastric secretions, aiding the digestion of rich baked goods.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory properties
items.content: Clove contains eugenol, which has notable anti‑inflammatory activity.

items.title: Blood‑sugar regulation
items.content: Cinnamon may help maintain more stable glucose levels after consuming sweet pastries.

items.title: Improved circulation
items.content: Ginger can dilate blood vessels, enhancing blood flow.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cinnamon, clove, or ginger.

items.title: Toxicity at high doses
items.content: Nutmeg exceeding 5 g can cause nausea, dizziness, and even hallucinations.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: Excessive ginger may cause heartburn in people with high stomach acidity.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Cinnamon can enhance the effect of anticoagulant medications, so intake should be limited when using such drugs.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add spices to the batter or frosting in small amounts (typically ½‑1 tsp per 500 g of dough). They can also be sprinkled on finished cakes for extra aroma. When using ground spices, incorporate them with the dry ingredients for even distribution.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store spices in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored, they retain their flavor for 2‑3 years. Keep them away from moisture to prevent mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Skin‑less chicken prepared by sautéing belongs to lean poultry meat. The NS (non‑specified) part usually refers to breast, thigh or fillet. Sautéing without skin retains most of the protein while keeping the fat content low.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide.
Sautéing without skin creates a crisp exterior while keeping the interior juicy.
Chicken is rich in B‑vitamins, especially B3 (niacin) and B6 (pyridoxine).
Compared with red meat, chicken contains less saturated fat.
Different cuisines use a variety of spices to flavor sautéed chicken.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides a complete set of essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Removing the skin dramatically reduces saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: B3 and B6 vitamins aid energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: The protein in chicken is quickly digested and absorbed by the body.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals can develop allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding salt or sauces can raise sodium levels, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature frying can produce acrylamide, a compound to limit with frequent consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skin‑less sautéed chicken can be served as a main dish, added to salads, sandwiches, pastas, or used in Asian‑style recipes. Use a small amount of oil and cook until golden brown for best texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh chicken should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C and used within 2 days. Frozen chicken retains quality for up to 9 months at –18 °C. Thaw frozen meat in the fridge before cooking.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese, made with animal fat or meat drippings (1983)

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of eggs, cheese, and animal fat (such as butter, lard, or meat drippings). Eggs are beaten and cooked in a pan with the fat, then grated cheese is folded in. This preparation is typical of traditional cuisines where animal fats were readily available.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the oldest foods known to humanity.
The cheese can range from soft cottage cheese to hard cheddar.
Animal fat enhances flavor and aroma but also raises the calorie count.
In 1983 this dish was commonly served in cafeterias and home kitchens as a quick, hearty breakfast.
Traditionally omelets were cooked in cast‑iron skillets, which provided even heat distribution.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs and cheese provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamins D and B12
items.content: Animal fat and eggs contain vitamin D, while cheese supplies vitamin B12, both important for nervous system function and blood formation.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The dish supplies calcium from cheese and phosphorus from eggs, supporting bone health.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Fat offers a quick source of energy, useful during periods of high physical activity.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Cooking with animal fat increases saturated fat levels, which may affect cholesterol when consumed frequently.

items.title: Allergy to eggs or dairy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs or cheese.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively high in calories; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol, so people with elevated cholesterol should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beat the eggs, season with salt and pepper, heat a pan with a small amount of animal fat, pour in the eggs, and when they begin to set, sprinkle grated cheese and continue cooking to the desired doneness. Serve hot, optionally garnished with herbs or vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best eaten fresh. If needed, store in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in an airtight container. Reheat in a pan or microwave, adding a little fat to prevent drying out.

ham-sandwich-or-sub-with-cheese-restaura.title: Ham Sandwich or Sub with Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A ham sandwich or sub with cheese is a popular fast‑food item consisting of a soft roll, sliced ham, melted or firm cheese, and often vegetables and sauces. It is commonly served in quick‑service restaurants, including the "1742" chain.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ham and cheese sandwiches became popular in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient work lunch.
The ham used is usually pork, but turkey or chicken versions are also available.
Cheese is often chosen to be processed so it melts quickly with a brief warm‑up.
At "1742" locations the sandwich is offered hot or cold, sometimes with crispy bacon added.
A sub (long roll) is convenient for serving larger portions suitable for groups.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Ham and cheese provide complete proteins essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cheese supplies calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Ham offers heme iron, which aids oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The sandwich delivers quick calories, useful for active lifestyles.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ham and whole‑grain rolls provide B12 and other B‑vitamins important for the nervous system.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed ham often contains a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese and ham contain saturated fats that should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to dairy may react to the cheese.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Some hams are cured with nitrites, which in large amounts are considered undesirable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be enjoyed hot, lightly toasted in an oven or microwave to melt the cheese. It is often served with fries, a side salad, or pickles. Add lettuce, tomato, or mustard to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared sandwich in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. If the roll is sliced, wrap it tightly in plastic to prevent drying. Keep ham and cheese separately in airtight containers.

spinach-frozen-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Spinach, frozen, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach is a leafy vegetable rich in vitamins and minerals. Frozen cooked spinach with no added fat retains most of its nutrients and is convenient for quick preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach belongs to the Amaranthaceae family and grows in temperate climates.
Freezing preserves up to 90 % of vitamin C and almost all folate.
Spinach contains plant sterols – carotenoids that become more bioavailable after heating.
In many cuisines spinach is used in pies, quiches, and stuffed dumplings.
Cooked spinach has lower oxalate levels than raw, making it safer for people prone to kidney stones.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Iron from spinach supports hemoglobin levels, especially when paired with vitamin C.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: One cup of cooked spinach provides fewer than 40 calories, helpful for weight management.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber promotes regular bowel movements and supports gut microbiota.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: High oxalate content may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, people may experience an allergic reaction to spinach.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salt is added during processing, sodium levels can rise; choose the unsalted version when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Frozen cooked spinach can be heated in the microwave or sautéed, added to soups, stews, omelets, pasta, or blended into a smooth puree.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in the freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After thawing, use within 2–3 days and do not refreeze.
